title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, runbooks
author: Priya Nair
body:
Summary
-------
This document is the canonical reference for the Redwood serving runtime: its high-level architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release and rollout guidance, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers owning model onboarding, runtime performance, and SREs responding to production incidents.

Scope
-----
- Runtime architecture and component responsibilities
- Kernel selection and scheduling policies
- Profiling methodology and playbooks for performance investigations
- Benchmarking suite, CI integration, and gold metrics
- Release notes process and safe rollout/rollback steps
- Known issues and mitigations
- On-call runbooks and team maintenance guidance

1) Architecture overview
------------------------
Intro: The serving runtime is composed of a lightweight front-proxy, request router, scheduler, kernel selection layer, execution engine (GPU kernels + kernel library), KV-cache manager, and telemetry/observability pipelines. The design targets 1) low tail latency for interactive workloads, 2) high throughput for bulk inference, and 3) predictable unit economics via batching and caching.

Components:
- Front Proxy (edge): TLS termination, API auth, rate limit enforcement, request validation.
- Router: routes requests to a runtime cluster by policy (latency SLO, region, model variant). Can route to hosted/dedicated/private endpoints.
- Scheduler: converts request stream into execution units (batches), selects kernels and device assignments. Implements priority queues per SLO class.
- Kernel Selector: maps model ops and sequence-length distribution to an ordered list of preferred kernels (FP16, INT8/4 quantized kernels, fused attention kernels).
- Execution Engine: launches CUDA/ROCm kernels, manages KV cache and attention state, and performs token decoding.
- KV/Prefix Cache: per-model prefix caching and shared cache shards for high-reuse prefixes.
- Observability: per-request end-to-end tracing, token-level cost/latency breakdown, GPU metrics, and internal perf events.

Diagram (text):
- [FRONT PROXY] -> [ROUTER] -> [SCHEDULER] -> [KERNEL SELECTOR] -> [EXECUTION ENGINE + KV CACHE] -> [OBSERVABILITY & METRICS]

Design principles:
- Predictable SLOs: request classification and admission control to protect latency-sensitive traffic.
- Cost-awareness: scheduler tracks tokens/GPU-second cost estimate to prefer cheaper compatible kernels for batch workloads.
- Compatibility: kernel selection maintains fallback compatibility matrix per model family.

2) Kernel scheduling and policies
--------------------------------
Goals: minimize tail latency for interactive requests while maintaining high GPU utilization for throughput workloads.

Key concepts:
- Scheduling classes: interactive (p50 latency target), bulk (throughput optimized), background (low priority).
- Isolation primitives: soft reservations for interactive classes; hard preemption disabled by default — we prefer admission control + opportunistic co-location.
- Kernel priority list: a model configuration contains an ordered list of kernels (e.g., fused-attn-fp16, attn-fp16, attn-int8) with compatibility tags.

Scheduler algorithm (simplified):
1. Classify request -> determine class and sequence-length estimate.
2. Consult admission controller: if interactive and queueing time + estimated exec time > latency SLO -> reject/apply fallback model variant.
3. If admitted, attempt to assemble batch up to max_batch_size for that kernel; batch time-window defaults to 8ms for interactive, 60–200ms for bulk (configurable).
4. Select highest-priority kernel compatible with the batch's token/sequence distribution and hardware capabilities.
5. Allocate device memory and KV cache slots; submit to execution engine.

Config table (defaults):
| key | default | description |
|-----|---------|-------------|
| max_batch_size_interactive | 32 | Max tokens per batch for interactive class |
| max_batch_size_bulk | 1024 | Max tokens per batch for bulk class |
| batch_time_window_interactive_ms | 8 | Max wait time to form a batch for interactive |
| batch_time_window_bulk_ms | 200 | Batch aggregation window for bulk workloads |
| kernel_fallback_strategy | ordered | Try kernels in order, fall back on compatibility |
| preempt_enabled | false | Preemption of running kernels is dangerous; use admission instead |

Tuning notes:
- Lower batch_time_window_interactive_ms for stricter p95 latency but inspect throughput drop.
- Use bulk class for offline batch scoring where throughput matters more than latency; set batch_time_window_bulk_ms >= 100ms.
- For models with long-context KV cache pressure, prefer smaller max_batch_size to avoid memory starvation.

3) Profiling playbook
---------------------
Purpose: Provide a repeatable playbook to identify CPU/GPU/IO hotspots, memory bottlenecks, and kernel-level inefficiencies.

Tools (approved):
- NVIDIA Nsight Systems / Nsight Compute (CUDA)
- ROCm profiling tools for AMD GPUs
- perf + BPF tracing for kernel/user-space latencies
- Triton/TF serving profilers if used as a shim
- tracers in the runtime (rtperf, internal event logs)

Profiling checklist:
1. Reproduce workload locally or on an isolated staging node with representative inputs. Capture baseline metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, GPU utilization, memory footprint, swap usage.
2. Run a system-level trace (nsys) for a 60–120s window capturing the failing workload.
3. Run kernel-level profiling (nsight compute) for the slow kernels identified; capture SM occupancy, achieved memory bandwidth, and instruction stats.
4. Inspect host-side traces for CPU scheduling stalls, syscalls, or memory thrashing.
5. Cross-check scheduler logs: batch formation times, admission rejections, kernel selection decisions.
6. Iterate: change single variable (kernel, batch size, quantization) and re-run to measure delta.

Example commands (CUDA):
- nsys profile --sample=cpu --trace=cuda,nvtx -o run_profile.qdrep ./run-inference-bench
- ncu --export run.ncu-rep --metrics=sm_efficiency, gld_throughput ./slow-kernel-bench

Profiling report template (must be attached to incident/ticket):
- Context: model, input shape distribution, traffic class, cluster config
- Baseline metrics and expected baselines
- Top 5 hotspots (by wall time) with suggested action
- Kernel-level recommendations (change kernel, fusions, input packing)
- Action plan and owner

4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration
--------------------------------------
The benchmarking suite is designed to exercise the runtime across model families, sequence-length distributions, and deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private). Benchmarks are run nightly and before every major runtime release.

Key components:
- Harness: reproducible runner that can drive multi-client traffic profiles and record latency/throughput.
- Datasets: synthetic token distributions, prompt-sets (from prompt-sets-and-benchmarks), and eval prompts used for quality checks.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory headroom, cost-per-token estimate.
- Baselines: for each model+hw profile we store a gold baseline. CI fails on >10% regression in p95 or >15% regression in throughput without documented justification.

Sample benchmark config (YAML text):
"""
model: redwood-7b-v2
hardware: a100-80gb
traffic_profile:
  - class: interactive
    concurrency: 100
    seq_len_dist: [16, 32, 64]
  - class: bulk
    concurrency: 200
    seq_len_dist: [512, 1024]
metrics: [p50, p95, p99, throughput_tokens_s, gpu_util]
"""

Reporting and dashboards:
- Nightly benchmark outputs are uploaded to the perf dashboard (dashboards-and-alerts) with per-route and per-model trend lines.
- CI gating: PRs that touch scheduler or kernel-selection code must include local benchmark results; failing PRs require reviewer signoff.

5) Release notes, rollout and compatibility guidance
---------------------------------------------------
Release tagging and compatibility:
- Each runtime release is tagged with a semver and a compatibility matrix mapping model versions to kernel variants. Breaking kernel changes must be flagged as Major.

Rollout plan (standard):
1. Merge -> Canary build (internal canaries on low-traffic cluster)
2. Run smoke benchmarks and golden prompt-set evals
3. Canary to 5% of traffic with enhanced tracing
4. Monitor p95/p99 latency and error-rate for 24–72 hours
5. Incrementally increase to 25%, then 75% with acceptance gates
6. Full rollout with scheduled maintenance window if baseline changes are large

Rollback guidance:
- Immediate rollback if p99 latency regresses by >30% or error rate >0.5% for critical routes.
- Preserve the previous kernel artifacts and configuration to allow quick revert.

Release note contents (template):
- Summary of changes (kernel updates, scheduler tuning, bug fixes)
- Affected models and hardware profiles
- Migration steps and config flags to opt-in/out
- Performance deltas vs baseline (table)

6) Known issues and mitigations (select examples)
------------------------------------------------
- ISSUE-2027-081: intermittent p99 spikes on long-context models (>=8k).
  - Symptom: p99 spikes under mixed interactive+bulk load.
  - Root cause: KV cache thrashing and memory fragmentation on device.
  - Workaround: Pin long-context traffic to dedicated nodepools; lower interactive max_batch_size.
  - Priority: high; ETA for fix: 2028-01-15 (kernel-level allocator improvements).

- ISSUE-2028-011: fallback kernel selects slower FP16 kernel for small batches on some A100 drivers.
  - Symptom: unexpected throughput drop for batch sizes <=16.
  - Workaround: set kernel_preference_override: fused-attn-fp16 for target nodepool.
  - Priority: medium; driver patch planned.

- ISSUE-2026-204: profiler overhead alters timing for very short workloads.
  - Symptom: profiling changes observed p50 by up to 8%.
  - Workaround: use longer capture windows and synthetic steady-state traffic for accurate measurement.
  - Priority: low.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)
------------------------------------------
Incident triage (p95/p99 regression):
1. Confirm: check perf dashboard and logs to validate regression and scope (single model, route, or cluster-wide).
2. Classify: Is this a config/regression or a hardware/driver issue?
3. Immediate mitigation: divert interactive class to fallback model variant or reduce max_batch_size_interactive via feature flag.
4. Hotfix: if needed, pin nodepool to previous runtime binary and drain/update cluster.
5. Root cause analysis: follow profiling playbook and open postmortem.

Node OOM / KV cache exhaustion:
- Symptoms: OOM errors, failed allocations, or slowdowns due to swapping.
- Mitigation steps:
  1. Temporarily reduce per-model max_context_length or lower batch sizes via runtime flags.
  2. Drain non-critical workloads to other nodepools.
  3. If repeated, escalate to runtime-kernel team for allocator and fragmentation fixes.

On-call checklist (quick):
- Pager receiver: check p95/p99 latency, error rate, GPU memory headroom, and recent deploys.
- If deploy triggered issue: rollback to previous release.

8) Team wiki & ownership
------------------------
- Ownership: runtime-architecture (team) owns kernel selection, scheduler, and execution engine. SRE owns runbooks and incident response.
- On-call: rotation documented in eng-sre/runbooks; runtime team provides secondary support for kernel-level issues.
- Doc cadence: major doc updates at each release; profiling playbook reviewed quarterly.

Maintenance tasks (monthly):
- Verify CI benchmark baselines and update gold metrics when model or hw changes occur.
- Run a smoke canary after kernel library updates.
- Re-run the profiling regression suite against a subset of models to detect silent regressions.

Appendices
---------
A) Example runtime config snippet (yaml):
"""
runtime:
  scheduler:
    max_batch_size_interactive: 32
    batch_time_window_interactive_ms: 8
    max_batch_size_bulk: 1024
    batch_time_window_bulk_ms: 200
  kernel_selection:
    strategy: ordered
    preference: [fused-attn-fp16, attn-fp16, attn-int8]
  admission_control:
    interactive_latency_slo_ms: 120
    rejection_policy: fallback_model_variant
"""

B) Useful CLI commands:
- tail -n 200 /var/log/runtime/runtime.log | jq '.message' | grep model-id
- curl -sS http://localhost:9090/debug/scheduler | jq
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx -o profile.qdrep ./integration-bench

C) Contacts and escalation
- runtime-architecture@redwood.com (primary)
- eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com (pager)
